title: Cello Suite No. 1 in G major
hook: One cello, alone, playing melody, bass and harmony at once, beginning with the best-known prelude ever written for it.

painting.title: Portrait of a Cello Player
painting.pairingNote: A working musician of Bach’s own generation, painted in Lombardy around 1740 with his hand on the neck of a Baroque cello, the instrument these suites were written for.

facts: Bach most likely wrote the six cello suites between 1717 and 1723, when he was music director at the court of Prince Leopold in Köthen. No copy in his own hand survives. The main source is a copy made by his second wife, Anna Magdalena Bach, headed *Suites à Violoncello Solo senza Basso*: suites for cello alone, without a bass.

A [[suite|suite]] is a set of dances in one key. Each of Bach’s six opens with a prelude and then follows the same order: [[allemande|allemande]], [[courante|courante]], [[sarabande|sarabande]], a pair of lighter dances (in this suite, two minuets) and a [[gigue|gigue]] to finish.

A cello mostly plays one note at a time, yet Bach makes it sound like several instruments. Broken chords, low notes that ring on under the tune and leaps between registers let the ear fill in a bass line and a harmony that are only hinted at.

For a long time the suites were little known and rarely played in public; many saw them as studies. The cellist Pablo Casals found an edition in a Barcelona shop as a boy of 13, played them in public for years and made the first complete recording: Suite No. 1 was recorded in Paris in June 1938.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a ripple of broken chords (I), a flowing conversation (II), a quick run (III), a slow dance in chords (IV), two minuets, the second in the minor (V), a jig to end (VI).

movements.heading: Prélude
movements.summary: The famous one. A single pattern of broken chords, rising and falling, repeats bar after bar while the harmony changes underneath. Halfway through the music comes to rest, then sets off again, more restless, and builds through a long climb over one repeated low note to a full, ringing close.

mainIdeas.name: The ripple
mainIdeas.description: each bar is one chord played as a wave of notes, starting from a low note, rising and falling back.

mainIdeas.name: The climb
mainIdeas.description: near the end, a low note sounds again and again while the notes above it creep upwards, step by step.

stops.hear: A wave of notes rising from the cello’s low G and falling back, the same shape in every bar
stops.happening: The home chord, G major, spread out as an [[arpeggio|arpeggio]] on the open strings

stops.hear: The wave keeps its shape but the chords begin to darken and lead away from home
stops.happening: The harmony moves towards new keys

stops.hear: The music settles on a chord and seems to pause for breath
stops.happening: Halfway: a resting point on D, the key a fifth above G

stops.hear: The pattern breaks up into runs and wider leaps; the mood is more searching
stops.happening: The second half wanders further from home

stops.hear: One low note keeps sounding between the moving notes, while the line above it climbs slowly upwards
stops.happening: A long [[pedal-note|pedal note]] on D: the tension builds

stops.hear: The climb reaches the top; broad chords sweep across all four strings

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A last, full G major chord

notice: In the first bars, listen for the lowest note of each wave. Those notes, one per bar, make a slow bass line of their own.
Before the climax, notice how often the same low D returns, like a drone under the rising line.

movements.heading: Allemande
movements.summary: A moderate dance in four, though nobody would dance to it now: a continuous, flowing line of quick notes, with a few chords for weight. Like every dance in the suite it has two halves, and each half is played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The flowing line
mainIdeas.description: running notes that move mostly by step, with an upbeat into each phrase.

stops.hear: A short upbeat, then a calm, unbroken stream of notes
The opening comes back
The stream starts again from a new note and moves through other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The line settles on a low G

notice: Listen for the moment the second half begins: it starts like the first, but from a different note.

movements.heading: Courante
movements.summary: “Running.” A quicker dance in three, full of energy, with fast notes that leap across the strings. Two halves again, each repeated.

mainIdeas.name: The run
mainIdeas.description: quick notes that bounce between low and high, with a firm accent at the start of each bar.

stops.hear: A brisk, bright line in three beats
The opening again
The music moves away from home, with sharper leaps
The second half again

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A clean close on G

notice: Notice how the line jumps between a low note and a high one, so that one cello seems to play two parts in turn.

movements.heading: Sarabande
movements.summary: A slow, dignified dance in three, played in chords. In a [[sarabande|sarabande]] the weight often falls on the second beat of the bar, which gives it a stately, lingering step.

mainIdeas.name: The chords
mainIdeas.description: two or three notes sounded at once, as [[double-stop|double stop]]s and broken chords, with a slow tune on top.

stops.hear: Slow, full chords; the music leans on the middle beat of each bar
The opening phrase again
The tune rises higher and moves into other keys
The second half again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A soft, final chord on G

notice: Count the beats in three. You may feel the second beat as the strongest, which is the mark of a sarabande.

movements.heading: Menuet I – Menuet II
movements.summary: Two minuets, light dances in three. The first is bright and in G major; the second turns to G minor and is one of only five movements in all six suites written as a single line, with no chords at all. Then the first minuet returns.

mainIdeas.name: Menuet I
mainIdeas.description: a cheerful tune with chords on the strong beats.

mainIdeas.name: Menuet II
mainIdeas.description: a quieter, more wistful tune in the minor, one note at a time.

stops.hear: A graceful tune in three, with some chords
The tune moves on, then comes back to its start
stops.happening: The second half of Menuet I, with repeats

stops.hear: The mood darkens: a gentle tune in the minor, with no chords
The bright first tune again
stops.happening: Menuet I returns, usually without its repeats

notice: Compare the two minuets. The first has chords; the second is one bare line, and it sounds more private.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: On Spotify this track is wrongly labelled “Menuet I – VI. Bourrée II”. It contains both minuets.

movements.heading: Gigue
movements.summary: A fast, skipping jig in groups of three notes, the usual way to end a suite. It is short and cheerful, and over in two minutes.

mainIdeas.name: The jig
mainIdeas.description: a bouncing long-short rhythm, quick and light.

stops.hear: A quick, skipping tune in a long-short rhythm
The first part again
The tune moves into new keys and grows busier

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A bright, firm close on G
stops.happening: The suite ends where it began

notice: Tap the beat: the notes fall in threes, long-short, the lilt of a jig.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Pierre Fournier recorded all six suites for Deutsche Grammophon’s early-music label, Archiv Produktion, in the Beethovensaal in Hanover in December 1960. The set has been reissued many times since it first appeared in 1961.

threads.title: One instrument, many voices
threads.body: Bach writes for a single cello, but almost every movement suggests a bass, a tune and the harmony between them. The listener’s ear does the rest.

threads.title: The open G
threads.body: The cello’s two lowest strings are C and G, and this suite in G major keeps returning to the resonance of the open G string, from the first note of the prelude to the last chord of the gigue.

threads.title: A dance suite
threads.body: Allemande, courante, sarabande, minuets and gigue were real dances of the time, in a fixed order. Bach keeps their rhythms but turns them into music for listening.
